Brian uses Manannán’s self-directing boat, obtained through Lugh, during the lethal quest.
One later recension names Brian as her son by Delbaeth.
One genealogy makes Brian Ogma's descendant through Delbaeth.

Brigit.note: Learned Dagda genealogy permits Brigit to be described as Aengus’s sister.
Their union is not narrated, but both are explicitly named as Rúadán’s parents.
Brigit is explicitly identified as the Dagda’s daughter.

Brigit the woman of healing.note: She is one of Brigit's two identically named sisters.

Brigit the woman of smithcraft.note: She is one of Brigit's two identically named sisters.

Brân Bendigeidfran.note: The Welsh Manawydan is Brân’s brother.
Manawydan fights beside Brân in Ireland and becomes one of seven survivors.

Bríg.note: Bríg arrives and keens after Goibniu kills her son Rúadán.

Buach.note: Some inconsistent Irish genealogies associate Buach with Lug as a consort.

Buarainech.note: A variant genealogical tradition names Buarainech as Balor’s father.

Bé Chuille.note: Bé Chuille enchants trees, stones, and sods to terrify the Fomorian host.

Bé Find.note: Bé Find, the supernatural mother of Fráech, is Boann’s sister.

Bé Finn.note: Bé Finn is associated with Donn’s uncertain maternal or foster-parental genealogy.

Bói.note: Some inconsistent Irish genealogies associate Bói with Lug as a consort.

Búi.note: Búi is a localized wife of Lugh associated with Cnogba.
One tradition says Búi commits adultery with Cermait, provoking Lugh’s retaliation.

Caer Ibormeith.note: Aengus recognizes Caer, becomes a swan, and flies with her to the Brug.

Cai.note: Cai and Manawydan both belong to Arthur’s company, without a private exchange.

Cairbre mac Étaín.note: Lug asks Cairbre’s contribution; Cairbre promises satire and magical verbal action.

Campestres.note: Epona appears beside the parade-ground goddesses in cavalry dedications.

Caradog Freichfras.note: A late genealogical note makes Caradog Gwyn's brother through a shared mother.

Casmáel.note: The Fomorian Ochtríallach kills Casmáel during the battle.

Castor.note: Their images appear on separate faces of the same monument.

Castor and Pollux.myth: Pillar of the Boatmen divine assemblage
Castor and Pollux.note: The divine twins and Esus share the monument without interaction.

Caswallawn.note: While Brân is absent, Caswallawn kills his regents and usurps his British kingdom.
Several medieval traditions identify Caswallawn as Beli’s son.

Caswallawn fab Beli.note: Variant triadic lists juxtapose them without recording a direct encounter.

Caswallon.note: The wider learned British genealogy makes Caswallon a brother of Lludd.

Caswallon son of Beli.note: Caswallon, Manawydan’s cousin, usurps Britain; Manawydan refuses to contest him.

Celeia.note: Epona and the local goddess Celeia are jointly honored with Jupiter.

Cermait.note: Cermait is named as a son of the Dagda.
A later tale says the Dagda revives or preserves Cermait with a healing staff.

Cermait Cóem.note: Cermait and Aengus are grouped among the Dagda’s sons.
Cermait joins Aengus and Áed in killing Lug.

Cermait Milbél.note: Lugh kills Cermait over an alleged affair with Lugh’s wife.

Cethen.note: Cethen is recurrently named among Dían Cécht’s sons.
Some genealogies make Cethen, Cian’s brother, Lugh’s paternal uncle.

Cethlenn.note: Early-modern mythography presents Cethlenn as Balor’s wife.
Some traditions say he eventually dies from Cethlenn’s battle wound.

Cian.note: Balor gives his daughter Ethne to Cian in a formal alliance.

Cian.myth: Death of the avenging grandson’s father
Cian.note: In Donegal folklore, Balor or his agents kill the child’s father, often by beheading.
Gavida and Mac Kineely are brothers; Gregory renames them Goibniu and Cian.
Cian, son of Dian Cécht, is Lugh’s father.
Lugh investigates Cian’s murder and exacts lethal compensation from his killers.
Lug is Cian’s son and later avenges his murder.

Cigfa.note: Manawydan and Cigfa survive together, practice crafts in England, and return to Dyfed.

Cirb.note: The king of rams is owned or accompanied by Brigit.

Clíodhna.note: This Munster Otherworld woman was later included among regional fairy queens.

Cnú Deireoil.note: Interpolated or genealogical material names Cnú Deireoil as Lugh’s son.

Cnú Deireóil.note: Genealogical or place-lore traditions name Cnú Deireóil among Lug’s obscure offspring.

Coirpre mac Étaine.note: After Bres denies him proper hospitality, Coirpre’s satire destroys Bres’s prosperity and helps end his reign.

Coirpre mac Étaíne.note: Coirpre’s satire destroys Bres’s prosperity and kingly legitimacy after receiving inadequate hospitality.

Conn.note: Conn is Lir and Aobh’s son.
Lir reunites with Conn in swan form and laments their separation.

Corand.note: Place-lore is interpreted as making Corand his son or protégé.

Coraniaid.note: Lludd destroys the supernaturally perceptive Coraniaid using Llefelys’s prescribed substance.

Credne.note: Lugh asks what battle service the bronze-worker Credne will provide.
Lug questions Credne, who promises rivets, shield-rims, and spear fittings.
Credne and Nuadu appear in the same divine councils or army.

Creiddylad.note: Nudd is named as Creiddylad’s father.
Creiddylad is named as the daughter of Lludd Silver-Hand.

Creiddylad ferch Lludd.note: Gwyn calls himself Creiddylad's lover; she is also his contested bride.
Gwyn carries Creiddylad away by force before her union with Gwythyr.
They become siblings only if the disputed identification of Nudd with Lludd is accepted.

Crédne.note: Genealogical arrangements make Crédne his brother or craft-relative.
Some accounts pair Dían Cécht’s medicine with Crédne’s craftsmanship.
Crédne continuously renews weapons used against the Fomorian host.
Crédne makes rivets and fittings for Goibniu’s weapons.
Crédne supplies rivets for the spear whose point Goibniu makes.
Crédne assists Dían Cécht in making or fitting Nuada's silver hand.

Crón.note: Crón grinds the spear assembled from Goibniu and the craftsmen’s components.

Curcog.note: Later material names Curcog as Manannán’s daughter and household member.

Cymidei Cymeinfoll.myth: The giant refugees and the cauldron
Cymidei Cymeinfoll.note: Brân shelters Cymidei and receives the resurrection cauldron from her and Llasar.

Cáelte mac Rónáin.note: Cáelte kills Lir during a violent encounter.

Cían.note: Cían is repeatedly identified as Dían Cécht’s son.
Cían.source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; Cath Maige Tuired

Cían.note: Balor gives Ethniu to Cían as part of an alliance.

Cú.note: Cú is recurrently named among Dían Cécht’s sons.
Some genealogies make Cú, Cian’s brother, Lugh’s paternal uncle.

Cú Chulainn.note: Lugh says he caused Deichtine’s pregnancy and foretells that her son will be Sétanta.
Lugh identifies himself as Cú Chulainn’s father, induces sleep, and heals his wounds.
Lug explicitly identifies himself as Cú Chulainn’s divine father.

Cú Chulainn.myth: Lug aids Cú Chulainn during the Táin
Cú Chulainn.note: Lug heals his exhausted son and fights in his place for three days.

Cú Chulainn.myth: Separation of Cú Chulainn and Fand
Cú Chulainn.note: Manannán places his mantle between Cú Chulainn and Fand, preventing their reunion.
They exchange threats before she foretells her later attacks in animal forms.
She professes love and offers possessions, cattle, and aid; he rejects her.
She attacks during his combat with Lóch; he wounds each animal form.
Disguised as an old milker, she obtains blessings that heal her wounds.
She breaks his chariot attempting to prevent his foretold fatal journey.
Later traditions identify the death-bird alighting near the slain hero as her.

Cŵn Annwn.note: Later Welsh poetry associates Gwyn with the supernatural hounds of Annwn.

Dabilla.note: Boann’s lapdog follows her, is swept away, and becomes two offshore rocks.

Dea Patrono.note: A modern cosmology makes Sucellus act with Dea Patrono as co-creators.

Delbaeth.note: Learned genealogies place Bres among Delbaeth’s descendants through Elatha or Elada.
One genealogy groups the Dagda and Delbaeth as sons of Elathan.
Certain recensions give Delbaeth as the Morrígan’s father.
One late genealogy makes Delbaeth progenitor of her sons.
The Auraicept makes Ogma, Bres, and Delbaeth brothers.
One extended pedigree makes Delbaeth an ancestor of Ogma.
Book of Leinster genealogies alternatively make Delbaeth Ogma's son.

Delbáeth.note: Boann is named as Delbáeth’s daughter.
Danand is named as Delbáeth’s daughter in one genealogy.

Delbáeth.myth: Conception of Brian, Iuchar and Iucharba
Delbáeth.note: Delbáeth fathers three sons upon his daughter Danand.
Cath Maige Tuired directly identifies Ériu as Delbáeth’s daughter.
Some Lebor Gabála passages also simplify Ériu’s ancestry to Delbáeth’s daughter.
Genealogies making Fiachna her father consequently make Delbáeth her grandfather.

Diana Venatrix.note: Diana appears beside some wider mallet-god figures conditionally identified as Sucellus.

Diana of the Scythians.note: Lucan compares Taranis's cruel altar with hers; the deities never meet.

Diarmait Ua Duibne.note: Aengus repeatedly advises and magically assists Diarmait during his flight.
Aengus carries Diarmait’s corpse to the Brug and sometimes temporarily revives him.

Donn Cúailnge.note: Müller-Lisowski controversially proposed that the Brown Bull represents an older Donn.
In bird form she warns the divine bull through an obscure prophecy.

Dormarch.note: Dormarch is described as Gwyn's finest hound, formerly belonging to Maelgwn.

Dot.note: Genealogical formulations name Dot, son of Nét, as Balor’s father.

Dylan.note: Dylan is delivered immediately before Lleu during Arianrhod’s virginity test.
Math is Dylan’s great-uncle through Arianrhod and the family of Dôn.
Math names the newborn Dylan and has him baptized after observing his sea-nature.

Dylan Eil Ton.note: Arianrhod gives birth to Dylan during Math's wand test.
Dylan is Gwydion’s nephew through his sister Arianrhod.
Gwydion is present at Dylan’s birth but has no later exchange.

Dylan ail Don.note: As Gofannon, Goibniu’s Welsh counterpart is Dylan’s maternal uncle.
Gofannon kills his nephew Dylan with a cast blow.
Dylan and the hidden infant Lleu are co-born during Arianrhod’s magical test.

Díanann.note: Díanann enchants trees, stones, and sods to terrify the Fomorian host.

Echtach.note: Echtach appears as Lugh’s wife in localized genealogical tradition.
Variant Irish genealogies make Nuadu the son of Echtach or Etarlám.
Some learned genealogies name Nuada as Echtach's son.

Edern ap Nudd.note: Welsh tradition identifies Edern as Nudd's son.

Eenatun.note: An online cosmology claims Eenatun created a female version of Sucellus.

Efnysien.note: Brân declines to execute Efnysien, compensating Matholwch instead for his destructive act.

Efnysien.myth: Gwern’s murder and the cauldron battle
Efnysien.note: Efnysien causes the disastrous battle, then destroys the resurrection cauldron and dies.
Efnysien begins the feud and later kills Branwen’s son before her.
Efnysien is Manawydan’s maternal half-brother through Penarddun.
Both participate in the councils and disastrous war in Ireland.

Eithne.note: The text names Mac Óc’s mother as Eithne, or Bóand.

Elada.note: Boann is Delbáeth’s daughter and therefore Elada’s granddaughter.

Elatha.note: Elatha is Bres’s Fomorian father and recognizes him through the gold ring.

Elatha.myth: Bres appeals to his Fomorian father
Elatha.note: Elatha condemns Bres’s unjust kingship but directs him to Balor and Indech.
Major genealogies make the Dagda a son of Elatha.
Elatha becomes Ériu’s lover and fathers Bres with her.
Elatha gives Ériu a ring that later identifies their son.
Ogma is repeatedly named as the son of Elatha.
Elatha.source: Cath Maige Tuired; Lebor Gabála; Auraicept

Elcmar.note: Aengus obtains Elcmar’s Brug by interpreting a day and night as all time.
Boann, called Eithne, is Elcmar’s wife in this variant.

Elcmar.myth: Elcmar’s enchanted journey to Mag nInis
Elcmar.note: The Dagda sends Elcmar to Bres’s residence while magically compressing nine months into one day.
The Dagda sends Elcmar away under magical hunger, thirst, and darkness.
The Dagda helps Óengus convert Elcmar’s temporary grant into permanent possession.
An earlier Brug resident, he is displaced through the Dagda’s and Óengus’s stratagems.

Elestron.note: Elestron and Arianrhod are listed among Dôn's children.

Englec.note: Some learned genealogies assign Elcmar’s daughter Englec to the Dagda.

Eochaid mac Eirc.note: Bres attacks the Fir Bolg king during the battle.
Eochaid reportedly kills Bres, despite the text subsequently electing Bres as king.

Eogabal.note: Áine is consistently identified as Eogabal’s daughter in the principal Knockainey tradition.

Ernmas.note: Through the Anand–Morrígan identification, Anand is a daughter of Ernmas.
Developed genealogy names Ernmas as Ériu’s mother.
The Morrígan is named among Ernmas’s daughters.

Eros.note: Modern comparativists characterize Aengus as a Celtic Eros, not an ancient identification.

Esarg.note: Some genealogies name Esarg as Dían Cécht’s father.
Some genealogical recensions attach Goibniu and associated craftsmen to Esarg.

Esras.myth: Training in the northern city of Gorias
Esras.note: Esras teaches the Tuatha Dé in Gorias.

Etarlám.note: Some genealogies make Etarlám Nuada's grandfather through Echtach.

Ethal Anbúail.note: Caer’s father initially withholds her, then reveals her swan transformation conditions under coercion.

Ethliu.note: Ethliu, daughter of Balor, is Lugh’s mother.

Ethne.note: Ethne is Balor’s daughter and the mother of Lugh.
Balor gives Ethne to Cian as part of an inter-group alliance.

Ethniu.note: Ethniu is Balor’s daughter and therefore a descendant of the Fomorian royal line.
Lug is the son of Balor’s daughter Ethniu or Ethliu.

Eufydd.note: Eufydd and Arianrhod are listed among Dôn's children.

Euroswydd.note: Euroswydd imprisons Llŷr Llediaith as one of Britain’s Exalted Prisoners.

Fand.note: Fand is presented as Manannán’s wife or partner, though their status varies.

Fand.myth: Separation of Fand and Cú Chulainn
Fand.note: Manannán returns for Fand and places his mantle between the former lovers.

Fand.myth: Cú Chulainn and the Otherworld war
Fand.note: An Otherworld woman, she afflicts Cú Chulainn and later becomes his lover.

Fe.note: Fe is one of the royal oxen owned or accompanied by Brigit.

Fer Fí.note: Later genealogical summaries sometimes make Eogabal’s son Fer Fí Áine’s brother.

Fiachna mac Delbaíth.note: One genealogical arrangement names Fiachna as Ériu’s father.

Fiachra.note: Fiachra is Lir and Aobh’s son.
Lir reunites with Fiachra in swan form and laments their separation.

Finnbarr.note: Finnbarr and his companions seek the aged Lir’s counsel.

Fionn.note: Some disputed genealogies make a possibly conflated Nuada Fionn's ancestor through Muirne.

Fionn mac Cumhaill.myth: Fenian Áine loves and marries Fionn
Fionn mac Cumhaill.note: A namesake Áine loves or marries Fionn and sometimes bears his children.
Modern comparison and practice sometimes blend the cognately named supernatural hunters.

Fionnbharra.myth: War of the Munster and Connacht hosts
Fionnbharra.note: Donn Fírinne leads Munster’s supernatural forces against Fionnbharra’s Connacht host.

Fionnuala.note: Fionnuala is Lir and Aobh’s daughter.
Fionnuala reveals the swans’ identities and curse to her grieving father.

Fir Bolg.note: Nuadu fights among the Túatha Dé Danann against the Fir Bolg.
Nuada leads the Túatha Dé against the Fir Bolg for Ireland.
The Tuatha Dé defeat the Fir Bolg after negotiations over Ireland fail.

Flesc.note: Flesc is among Nechtan’s supernatural cupbearers guarding the fountain Boann approaches.
Flesc.source: Boand I; Boand II; Tochmarc Emire

Flidais.note: Variant genealogies make Danand a daughter or descendant of Flidais.

Fomoire.myth: Bres’s reign and the Fomorian tribute
Fomoire.note: Fomorian overlords exact produce and humiliating labor from the Tuatha Dé.
The Tuatha Dé defeat the Fomorian host through coordinated divine arts.

Fortuna Conservatrix.note: Fortuna Conservatrix and Apollo Belenus jointly received an inscribed offering.

Fráech.note: Boann equips her nephew with clothing, weapons, horses, hounds, entertainers, and gaming equipment.

Fuamnach.note: Fuamnach opposes Aengus’s protection of Étaín and blows Étaín away.
A mound-associated sorceress, she transforms and expels her rival Étaín.

Fódla.note: Fódla is named as Ériu’s sister in the threefold genealogy.
Both independently ask the Milesians to preserve their names for Ireland.

Gaidiar.note: Genealogical traditions name Gaidiar as a son of Manannán.

Gearóid Iarla.myth: Fairy bride bears the enchanted Earl
Gearóid Iarla.note: Fitzgerald folklore makes Áine mother of the magical or enchanted Gearóid Iarla.

Genius loci.note: Epona and the local Genius were jointly honored at Naix and elsewhere.

Genius loci.myth: Joint receipt of the Mainz dedication
Genius loci.note: The local Genius receives a dedication alongside Jupiter Optimus Maximus Sucaelus.

Geoffrey’s Belinus.note: Later interpreters conflate Beli with Geoffrey’s distinct king Belinus.

Gilfaethwy.note: Gilfaethwy is explicitly called son of Dôn.
Gilfaethwy is Math’s nephew and conducts royal circuits for him.
Gilfaethwy betrays Math by assaulting Goewin in Math’s chamber during the war.
Math transforms Gilfaethwy into hind, boar, and she-wolf before restoring him.

Gilfaethwy fab Dôn.note: Gilfaethwy and Arianrhod are children of Dôn, with no recorded meeting.
Gilfaethwy fab Dôn.source: Math uab Mathonwy; Bonedd yr Arwyr

Gilfaethwy fab Dôn.note: Gilfaethwy is Gwydion’s brother and fellow son of Dôn.
Gwydion engineers war so Gilfaethwy can assault Goewin.
The brothers become mating animal pairs and produce three sons.

Glas Gaibhleann.myth: Theft of the magical gray cow
Glas Gaibhleann.note: Balor steals or covets the inexhaustibly lactating supernatural cow.

Glifiau son of Taran.note: Glifiau is among the seven survivors who return with Branwen.

Gobannus.note: The Continental divine smith is identified as Goibniu’s cognate regional counterpart.

Gobán Saor.note: Balor employs or deals with the supernatural master builder.

Goewin.note: Goewin holds Math’s feet in her lap, sustaining his magical life-condition.
Math marries Goewin after her assault and grants her authority over his realm.

Gofannon.note: Gofannon is identified as a son of Dôn.
The Welsh smith figure is identified as Goibniu’s linguistically related regional counterpart.
Math Hen and Gofannon appear together in a poetic list without interaction.

Gofannon fab Dôn.note: Later genealogy makes Gofannon her sibling or close kinsman.

Gronw Pebr.note: Gwydion’s pursuit compels Gronw to negotiate with Lleu.
Gwydion refuses Gronw’s request that followers hold his protective stone.
Gronw wounds Lleu under the contrived conditions that transform him into an eagle.
Lleu compels Gronw to face a return cast and kills him through the shielding stone.
Gronw attacks Lleu under contrived liminal conditions, transforming the wounded Lleu into an eagle.
Restored Lleu casts a spear through Gronw’s shielding stone and kills him.

Gronw Pebyr.note: They fall mutually in love and sleep together while Lleu is absent.
Blodeuedd and Gronw collaborate for a year to arrange Lleu's spear attack.

Gruddieu son of Muryel.note: Gruddieu is among the seven survivors who return with Branwen.

Gwallog ap Lleenog.note: A late genealogical note makes Gwallog Gwyn's brother through a shared mother.

Gwawl son of Clud.note: Rhiannon helps Pwyll trap and humiliate Gwawl, securing his renunciation.
Her inexhaustible-bag stratagem tricks Gwawl into entering the bag.

Gwern.note: Gwern, son of Branwen and Matholwch, is Brân’s nephew.
Brân receives Gwern affectionately and accepts a settlement making the child king of Ireland.
Branwen bears Gwern, her son by Matholwch, in Ireland.

Gwydion fab Dôn.myth: Creation from oak, broom, and meadowsweet flowers
Gwydion fab Dôn.note: Gwydion and Math magically create and name Blodeuedd.
Gwydion condemns her for the shame and attempted killing inflicted upon Lleu.
Gwydion imposes nocturnality and perpetual harassment by other birds.

Gwydion fab Dôn.myth: Transformation of Blodeuedd into an owl
Gwydion fab Dôn.note: Gwydion changes Blodeuedd into an owl and renames her Blodeuwedd.

Gwythyr ap Greidawl.note: Gwyn defeats Gwythyr's army after abducting Creiddylad.
Arthur orders both rivals to fight each May Day until Doomsday.
The former rivals jointly advise Arthur about confronting Orddu.

Hafgan.note: Hafgan rules a rival Annwn kingdom and repeatedly fights Arawn.
Arawn arranges Hafgan’s death by instructing disguised Pwyll to strike only once.

Heilyn son of Gwyn Hen.note: Heilyn is among the seven survivors who return with Branwen.

Heimdallr.note: John Rhŷs proposed Heimdallr as a comparative equivalent of Gwyn.

Hekate.note: Eclectic modern pagan practice sometimes merges Hekate with the Morrígan.

Hercules.note: Hercules appears on another face of a monument bearing a Cernunnos-type figure.
Epona shared or received restoration of a Roman shrine with Hercules and Silvanus.

Herne.note: Modern occult and neopagan interpretations sometimes blend Gwyn with Herne.

Herne the Hunter.note: Modern writers fused Cernunnos with the horned Windsor hunter.

Hychddwn.note: As a sow paired with boar-shaped Gilfaethwy, Gwydion bears Hychddwn.

Hychdwn.note: Math changes the boar-born offspring into a human boy and names him Hychdwn.
Math becomes foster-father to Hychdwn and arranges his care.

Hyddwn.note: As a hind paired with stag-shaped Gilfaethwy, Gwydion bears Hyddwn.
Math changes the deer-born fawn into a human boy and names him Hyddwn.
Math becomes foster-father to Hyddwn and arranges his baptism and fostering.

Hyfaidd Hen.note: Rhiannon is identified as his daughter; he hosts her intended wedding.

Iarbonel the Soothsayer.note: The Tuatha Dé descend from Nemed through Iarbonel the Soothsayer.

Ilbrecc.note: Later Otherworld and Fenian traditions name Ilbrecc as Manannán’s son.
Ilbrecc’s love for Aoife motivates Iuchra’s spell and connects the tragedy to Manannán’s household.

Ilbrecc of Assaroe.note: Lir of Síd Fionnachaidh wages a great war against Ilbrecc.

Indech.note: Balor and Indech jointly mobilize the Fomorian host.
Indech compels or threatens the Dagda to consume an enormous porridge.

Indech mac Dé Domnann.myth: Fomorian expedition against the Túatha Dé
Indech mac Dé Domnann.note: Indech exacts tribute during Bres’s reign and later leads Bres’s invasion forces.
She promises to destroy Indech, though the text later credits Ogma.
Ogma meets the Fomorian king or champion Indech in single combat.
One strand says Ogma and Indech fall together in combat.
Their mutual fall implies that Indech also dies in their combat.

Iuchar.note: Variant learned genealogy names Iuchar as one of Brigit's sons.
Danand is named as Iuchar’s mother.
Lugh imposes perilous compensation on Iuchar and refuses healing until his wounds prove fatal.
Lug imposes a perilous compensation quest for Cian’s murder and later withholds the healing pigskin.
Iuchar uses Manannán’s self-directing boat, obtained through Lugh, during the lethal quest.
One later recension names Iuchar as her son by Delbaeth.
One genealogy makes Iuchar Ogma's descendant through Delbaeth.

Iucharba.note: Variant learned genealogy names Iucharba or Uar as Brigit's son.
Danand is named as Iucharba’s mother.
Lugh imposes perilous compensation on Iucharba and refuses healing until his wounds prove fatal.
Lug imposes a perilous compensation quest for Cian’s murder and later withholds the healing pigskin.
Iucharba uses Manannán’s self-directing boat, obtained through Lugh, during the lethal quest.
One later recension names Iucharba as her son by Delbaeth.
One genealogy makes Iucharba Ogma's descendant through Delbaeth.

Iuchra.note: Iuchra’s spell creates the crane whose skin Manannán later turns into a bag.

Iweriadd.note: Later genealogical tradition sometimes names Iweriadd as Llŷr’s wife.

Jupiter Dolichenus.note: Caelestis Brigantia and Jupiter Dolichenus jointly receive a dedication.

Jupiter Optimus Maximus.note: A Celeia inscription jointly honors Jupiter Optimus Maximus, Epona, and Celeia.

King of the Dogheads.note: Lir volunteers to oppose the fantastic king of the Dogheads.

Labraid Luathlám.myth: Cú Chulainn and the Otherworld war
Labraid Luathlám.note: His Otherworld court recruits Cú Chulainn to defeat supernatural enemies.

Lerina.note: Lerina’s divine pair with Lero prompted speculative modern comparison with Lir.

Lero.note: Modern comparisons tentatively equate Gaulish Lero with Lir from resemblance and marine geography.

Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid.myth: The giant refugees and the cauldron
Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid.note: Brân shelters Llasar and receives the resurrection cauldron from him and Cymidei.

Llassar Llaes Gyfnewid.note: Manawydan imitates Llassar’s azure coloring technique when making saddles and shields.

Llefelys.note: Llefelys is named as a son of Beli Mawr.
Lludd and Llefelys are brothers, ruling Britain and France respectively.
Lludd consults Llefelys, who prescribes remedies for Britain’s three plagues.
Lludd and Llefelys are brothers in medieval Welsh tradition.
Lludd consults Llefelys and follows his remedies for Britain's three plagues.

Lludd.note: Lludd is Beli’s son and inherits Britain after Beli dies.
Lludd is philologically associated with Nudd and comparatively identified with Nodens.

Lludd Llaw Ereint.note: Later genealogy sometimes identifies or confuses Gwyn's father Nudd with Lludd.

Llwyd Cil Coed.note: Llwyd captures Rhiannon and forces her to carry hay wearing an ass's collar.

Llwyd ap Cil Coed.note: Manawydan captures Llwyd’s transformed wife and bargains until Llwyd lifts Dyfed’s enchantment.
Manawydan captures Llwyd’s transformed wife and compels restitution and permanent immunity.

Llŷr.note: Brân is repeatedly identified as Llŷr’s son.
Llŷr is genealogically named as Branwen’s father.
Manawydan is consistently identified as the son of Llŷr.

Luchta.note: Genealogical arrangements make Luchta his brother or craft-relative.
Luchta continuously renews weapons used against the Fomorian host.
Luchta makes shafts for Goibniu’s spearheads.
Luchta supplies the shaft for the spear whose point Goibniu makes.
Lugh coordinates the carpenter Luchta’s work for the coming battle.
Lug questions Luchta, who promises shields and spear-shafts.

Lug.note: One learned recension says Aengus, Áed, and Cermait kill Lug.
Bres leads the Fomorian cause defeated by Lug and the Túatha Dé.
Bres teaches Lug when to plough, sow, and reap, securing his release.
Lug tricks Bres into drinking red bitter liquid from wooden cows as false milk.
Lug kills Bres with false milk or bog-stuff, contradicting the agricultural-release ending.
Lug.source: Carn Húi Néit; Lebor Gabála Érenn

Lug.note: Buí is Lug’s wife; identifying her with Caillech Bérri is disputed.
The Dagda attends Lug’s muster and delays the Fomorians at his command.
The Dagda, Lug, and Ogma recover the stolen harp from the Fomorian hall.
Lug kills the Dagda’s son Cermait, whom the Dagda then mourns.
Dían Cécht is Lug’s grandfather through his son Cían.

Lug.myth: Lug asks each specialist’s battle contribution
Lug.note: Dían Cécht promises Lug next-day restoration of all nonfatal wounds.
Lug is the maternal grandson of the Fomorian champion Balor.
Lug fights the Fomorian host and turns Balor’s destructive eye upon it.
Lug kills his Fomorian grandfather Balor with a sling stone.
Bres teaches Lug when to plough, sow, and reap in exchange for release.
Goibniu and Dían Cécht are described as Lug’s two kinsmen.

Lug.myth: Secret war council and forging at Mag Tuired
Lug.note: Lug summons and questions Goibniu, who promises infallible replacement weapons.
She declares her destructive powers to Lug and later strengthens his host.
Nuadu tests and recognizes Lug’s many arts before admitting him to Tara.
Nuadu yields the royal seat or battle command to the exceptionally skilled Lug.
Nuada admits Lug after learning that he possesses every necessary art.
Nuada exchanges seats with Lug so Lug can direct resistance to the Fomoire.
Ogma answers Lug's summons and promises to repel the enemy king.
Ogma joins Lug and the Dagda in obtaining battle equipment.
Ogma writes seven b-strokes warning about the removal of Lug's wife.
He receives Síd Rodrubán during the Dagda’s allocation of mound dwellings.
Later classification places Cú Chulainn’s divine father and helper among the mound people.
Lug.source: Táin Bó Cúailnge; Compert Con Culainn

Lugaid.note: Lugaid is named as Nuadu’s son and is killed in battle.

Lughaidh.note: Lir is identified as Lughaidh’s son.

Lám.note: Lám is among Nechtan’s supernatural cupbearers guarding the fountain Boann approaches.
Lám.source: Boand I; Boand II; Tochmarc Emire

Lí Ban.myth: Recruiting Cú Chulainn for the Otherworld war
Lí Ban.note: She serves as envoy between Labraid’s Otherworld court and Cú Chulainn.

Lóch Lethglas.note: The Fomorian king Indech summons his poet Lóch Lethglas to identify his attacker.

Lúam.note: Lúam is among Nechtan’s supernatural cupbearers guarding the fountain Boann approaches.
Lúam.source: Boand I; Boand II; Tochmarc Emire

Mabon.note: Modern comparativists equate Aengus with Mabon as a divine youthful son.

Mabon ap Modron.note: Mabon pursues the boar before Manawydan’s group closes upon it.

Mac Cecht.myth: Reign of the three Túatha Dé kings
Mac Cecht.note: Ériu appears with Mac Cecht among the three paired kings and queens.
Mac Cecht kills her son Méche and destroys his serpent-hearts.

Mac Cinnfhaelaidh.note: Later folklore replaces Cian with Mac Cinnfhaelaidh as Lugh’s father.

Mac Cuill.myth: Reign of the three Túatha Dé kings
Mac Cuill.note: Ériu appears with Mac Cuill among the three paired kings and queens.
Mac Cuill kills Lugh to avenge his father Cermait.
Mac Cuill and his brothers spear Lugh through the foot and drown him.

Mac Cécht.note: Mac Cécht joins his brothers in spearing and drowning Lugh to avenge Cermait.

Mac Gréine.note: Mac Gréine is named as Ériu’s husband and a Túatha Dé king.
Mac Gréine joins his brothers in spearing and drowning Lugh to avenge Cermait.

Mac Óc.note: Mac Óc fetches Dían Cécht, who answers the summons.

Macha.note: Balor kills Macha alongside Nuadu during the battle.
Through the Anand–Morrígan equation, Macha and Anand are daughters of Ernmas.
Modern comparativists identify or link them through horse and sovereignty motifs without textual proof.
Balor kills Macha daughter of Ernmas during the battle.
Macha supports or proclaims the Túatha Dé victory alongside Lug’s war effort.
Macha and the Morrígan are listed among Ernmas’s daughters.
They jointly cast mist, fire, and blood against the Fir Bolg.
A Macha is killed alongside Nuadu by Balor in the battle account.

Macha daughter of Ernmas.note: Macha falls beside Nuada at Balor's hands; no separate exchange is narrated.

Manawydan fab Llŷr.note: Triadic variants juxtapose them as golden shoemakers without depicting a meeting.

Maponos.note: Modern comparativists equate Aengus with Continental Celtic Maponos without ancient testimony.

Mars Cocidius.note: Named separately from Toutatis among the divine recipients of a vow.

Mars Segomo.note: A Lyon monument was reportedly dedicated to Epona and Mars Segomo.

Math mac Umair.note: Evans-Wentz reported a speculative comparison between Math and the Irish magician.

Matholwch.myth: Marriage alliance between Britain and Ireland
Matholwch.note: Brân accepts Matholwch’s proposal to marry Branwen and unite their kingdoms.
Brân gives Matholwch horses, precious objects, and the resurrection cauldron as reparations.
Brân invades Matholwch’s kingdom after Branwen’s abuse and the attempted suppression of her message.
Brân initially claims Matholwch’s kingdom before accepting a settlement making Gwern king.
Branwen marries Matholwch, king of Ireland, in a dynastic alliance.
Matholwch removes her from his chamber and permits or orders prolonged abuse.
This variant attributes a singular harmful blow directly to Matholwch.

Mathonwy.note: Math is named as Mathonwy’s son; no narrative about Mathonwy survives.

Matres.note: Modern comparative reconstructions sometimes identify Epona with the Matres; no universal ancient equation survives.

Meirchion.note: A later poem gives Blodeuwedd ordinary parentage as Meirchion's daughter.
Meirchion.source: Poem attributed to Dafydd ap Gwilym

Meirchion Llwyd.note: Anthony Powel's variant calls Blodeuwedd the daughter of Meirchion Llwyd.

Men.note: Men is one of the royal oxen owned or accompanied by Brigit.

Miach.note: Miach restores natural flesh over Nuadu’s injured limb in nine days.

Midir.note: Aengus courts Étaín for Midir and arranges completion of her bride-price.
Midir fosters Boann’s son Mac Óc; no direct conversation survives.

Midir.myth: Óengus’s upbringing and the Étaín complex
Midir.note: Midir is associated with Óengus’s fostering, though his relationship to the Dagda varies.
Dían Cécht completely heals Midir’s eye without scar or blemish.
Midir and his companions seek the aged Lir’s counsel.
The ruler of Brí Léith repeatedly crosses between mound and human courts.

Milucra.note: A probably distinct Fenian Áine and Milucra are described as sisters.
Áine and Milucra compete as rival sisters in love with Fionn.

Minawg.note: A disputed poetic reading may identify Minawg as Lleu’s son.

Moirai.note: A damaged dedication groups Epona with fate goddesses and a local Genius; the reading is debated.

Mongán.note: Manannán foretells and begets Mongán, then claims him three nights after birth.
Manannán raises Mongán under supernatural tutelage before returning him to humanity.

Morfessa.myth: Training in the northern city of Falias
Morfessa.note: Morfessa teaches the Tuatha Dé in Falias.

Morgan le Fay.note: Modern traditions sometimes merge them, though no medieval source identifies them.

Máeltne Mórbrethach.note: Máeltne rejects Bres’s perpetual milk and quarterly harvest offers and defines the proper seasonal cycle.

Méche.note: Méche, bearer of three destructive serpent-hearts, is identified as her son.

Méiche.note: Dían Cécht kills and burns the poisonous serpent-being Méiche.

Míach.note: Míach is securely identified as Dían Cécht’s son.
Míach.source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; Cath Maige Tuired

Míach.myth: Dían Cécht kills his superior healer son
Míach.note: After three healed wounds, Dían Cécht removes Míach’s brain.

Míach.myth: Physicians chant over the healing well Sláine
Míach.note: Míach joins Dían Cécht at Sláine despite his earlier narrated death.

Míach.myth: DanMachi medical rivalry and silver arm
Míach.note: DanMachi reimagines Dian Cecht and Miach as rival medical gods.
Míach helps operate the healing well that restores Fomorian opponents.
Míach replaces the prosthesis and regenerates Nuada's natural limb over nine days.

Nantosuelta.myth: Joint receipt of Bellausus’s vow at Sarrebourg
Nantosuelta.note: They appear together as paired figures receiving Bellausus’s votive dedication.
Modern scholarship conventionally interprets the securely paired goddess as Sucellus’s consort or parèdre.

Nantosuelta.myth: The pair walk and order a young world
Nantosuelta.note: Contemporary devotional myths make them order nature, teach agriculture, and protect households.

Nechtan.note: Boann is Nechtan’s wife in the principal Boyne poems.
Nechtan.source: Boand I; Boand II; Tochmarc Emire

Nemain.note: Learned traditions associate Nemain with the Morrígan in variable war-fury groupings.

Nemed.note: Fomorian leaders fight Nemed’s people and later subject them to catastrophic tribute.
Medieval genealogy makes the Tuatha Dé descendants of Nemed.

Niamh Chinn Óir.note: Modern retellings inconsistently identify Niamh as Manannán’s daughter.

Nisien.note: Nisien is Brân’s peaceful maternal half-brother.
Nisien accompanies Brân’s host during the Irish expedition.
Nisien is Manawydan’s maternal half-brother through Penarddun.

Nuadu Airgetlám.note: Balor kills Nuadu during the battle.

Nudd.note: Gwyn is consistently named as Nudd's son.
Nudd is considered a probable Welsh linguistic and mythological reflex of Nodens.

Numina Augustorum.note: A centurion dedicated one vow to Sulis Minerva and two emperors’ divine powers.

Nyarlathotep.note: Lovecraft reinvents Nodens as an elder supernatural power opposed to Nyarlathotep.

Nynniaw.note: Nynniaw is named as a son of Beli Mawr.

Nás.note: Nás is a localized wife of Lugh associated with Naas.
Nás’s death, burial, lamentation, and assembly are linked with Lugh.
Some inconsistent Irish genealogies associate Nás with Lug as a consort.

Nét.note: Balor is identified as Nét’s grandson.
Learned genealogies inconsistently place Bres among Nét’s descendants.
A pedigree makes Ogma son of Elatha son of Nét.

Núadu.note: Bres replaces the mutilated Núadu; after Núadu’s healing, Bres is deposed and Núadu resumes rule.
Balor kills Núadu Silverhand during the great battle.
Bres receives sovereignty after Núadu’s disqualification and loses it when Núadu recovers.
Goibniu joins the anti-Fomorian council convened around Lug and Núadu.

Núadu Airgetlám.myth: Núadu receives the articulated silver hand
Núadu Airgetlám.note: Dían Cécht fits Núadu with a silver hand moving naturally.
First-battle traditions credit Dían Cécht with Núadu’s silver replacement.
Núadu Airgetlám.source: Cath Maige Tuired Cunga; Lebor Gabála

Ochtríallach.myth: The Fomoire bury the healing well
Ochtríallach.note: Ochtríallach counters Dían Cécht’s healing work by ordering Sláine buried.

Octriuil.note: Octriuil is identified as Dían Cécht’s son within the tale.

Octriuil.myth: Physicians chant over the healing well Sláine
Octriuil.note: Father and son jointly chant over Sláine during the battle.
Octriuil helps operate the healing well that restores Fomorian opponents.

Odras.note: The Morrígan steals Odras’s bull for her own cow.
She chants spells over sleeping Odras and dissolves her into a stream.

Ogmios.note: Scholars reconstruct Ogma and Ogmios as related or identical figures.

Orddu.note: Gwyn advises Arthur who should confront Orddu; no direct combat occurs.

Orna.note: Ogma draws and cleans Orna, which then recounts its deeds.

Partholón.note: Cichol Gricenchos and his Fomorian followers fight Partholón, who defeats them.

Penarddun.note: Penarddun is genealogically named as Branwen’s mother.
Penarddun is named daughter of Beli son of Manogan.
Their union is inferred from their stated parentage of Bendigeidfran and Manawydan.
Later medieval reconstruction commonly treats Penarddun as Manawydan’s mother.

Pryderi.note: Arawn sends Pryderi a remarkable herd of Otherworld pigs.
Pryderi serves in Brân’s expedition and survives the battle.
Pryderi helps carry Brân’s head through Harlech and Gwales toward London.
Pryderi is among the seven survivors who return with Branwen.
Manawydan becomes Pryderi’s companion and stepfather after Pryderi arranges the marriage.
Manawydan compels Llwyd to free Pryderi from magical captivity.
Manawydan becomes Pryderi’s stepfather by marrying Rhiannon.
They survive Ireland, return together, hunt, work, and endure Dyfed’s enchantment.
Manawydan’s negotiations compel Llwyd to release the imprisoned Pryderi.
The poem says Manawydan and Pryderi know the ageless fortress Caer Siddi.
Pryderi.source: Song of the Sons of Llŷr

Pryderi.note: Gruffydd and Ford reconstruct Manawydan as Pryderi’s original father.
Math leads Gwynedd’s army against Pryderi after Gwydion steals the pigs.
Math permits Pryderi’s dispute with Gwynedd to be settled by single combat.
Rhiannon bears Pryderi, who is stolen at birth and later restored.
Rhiannon follows the immobilized Pryderi and becomes imprisoned alongside him.

Pryderi fab Pwyll.note: Gwydion exchanges temporary enchanted horses and dogs for Pryderi’s pigs.
Gwydion fraudulently obtains Pryderi’s Otherworld-derived swine.
Gwydion provokes war and meets Pryderi in single combat.
Gwydion kills Pryderi through strength and enchantment.

Pwyll.note: Pwyll drives Arawn’s hounds from their stag and appropriates the kill.
Arawn gives Pwyll his appearance for a year-and-a-day exchange of realms.
Their successful exchange establishes an enduring friendship and political alliance.
Arawn and Pwyll reciprocally exchange horses, hounds, hawks, treasures, and other gifts.
Rhiannon chooses Pwyll over Gwawl, marries him, and bears Pryderi.

Pwyll.myth: The horsewoman who could not be overtaken
Pwyll.note: She permits Pwyll to catch her only after he directly asks her to stop.
Rhiannon devises Pwyll's successful counter-plot against Gwawl.

Riocalatis.note: Named beside Toutatis on a damaged altar; its precise divine status remains uncertain.

Rosmerta.note: A probable Rosmerta image shares the monument with the probable Esus scene.

Ruadán.myth: Death of Ruadán and first keening
Ruadán.note: Bríg comes to the battlefield and keens over her slain son.

Rúadán.note: Rúadán, the Fomorian spy killed by Goibniu, is Bres and Brigit’s son.
Rúadán wounds Goibniu with a spear made by the divine craftsmen.
Goibniu pulls out the spear and hurls it through Rúadán.

Samthainn.note: Gavida and Mac Samthainn are brothers, retained as Goibniu and Samthainn by Gregory.

Semias.myth: Training in the northern city of Murias
Semias.note: Semias teaches the Tuatha Dé in Murias.

Silvana.note: Silvana accompanies male figures in the wider corpus, though their Sucellus identity is uncertain.

Smertios.myth: Pillar of the Boatmen divine assemblage
Smertios.note: Both beings occur on the same monument without interaction.

Smertrios.note: Their divine images occupy separate faces of the same monument.

Sol.note: Separate imperial dedications juxtapose Apollo Belenus and Sol without identifying them.

Sons of Míl.myth: The Sons of Míl invade Ireland
Sons of Míl.note: The Tuatha Dé negotiate and fight with the Sons of Míl, raising magical winds.

Sreng.note: Bres and Sreng meet as envoys, compare weapons, and exchange their armies’ demands.
Sreng fights Nuadu and severs his right arm at the shoulder.
Nuadu and Sreng later negotiate rather than fight under unequal conditions.
Nuada fights Sreng, who severs his hand or right arm.

Sreng.myth: Expanded First Battle of Mag Tuired
Sreng.note: Sreng cuts Nuada's right arm off at the shoulder with shield attached.

Tadg.note: Some Fenian genealogies make a possibly conflated Nuada an ancestor of Tadg.

Tailtiu.note: Lugh establishes or perpetuates an assembly and funeral games at Tailtiu’s burial place.
Tailtiu is Lug’s foster-mother in the dominant Lugnasad tradition.
After Tailtiu dies clearing land, Lug establishes games or an assembly at her grave.

Taliesin.note: Taliesin is among the seven survivors who accompany Brân’s living head.
Later poetry says Taliesin transforms Brân from miserliness to generosity.
Taliesin is among the seven survivors who return with Branwen.
Gwion tends Ceridwen’s cauldron fire as her assigned servant.
Ceridwen pursues Gwion through successive animal transformations after he gains the potion’s knowledge.
Ceridwen becomes a black hen and swallows Gwion after he becomes grain.
Ceridwen gestates swallowed Gwion for nine months and bears him as Taliesin.
Unable to kill the beautiful infant, Ceridwen seals him in a vessel and casts him away.
The Taliesin persona claims participation while Gwydion’s magic moves the trees.

Tarvos Trigaranus.note: Their reliefs appear separately on the same civic monument.

Tarvos Trigaranus.myth: The tree, bull, and three cranes
Tarvos Trigaranus.note: Esus cuts a tree beside or within a scene featuring the bull.
Tarvos Trigaranus.source: Pillar of the Boatmen and Trier relief

Tethra.note: Tethra joins Elatha and Indech among the Fomorian kings imposing tribute under Bres.
After battle Ogma finds and takes the Fomorian king Tethra's sword.

Teyrnon Twryf Liant.note: Teyrnon returns her lost son, ending Rhiannon's mounting-block penance.
Rhiannon and Pwyll reward Teyrnon after he restores Pryderi.

The King of the Green Isle.note: He explains Beira’s imprisonment of Bride and advises Angus.

The three gods of Danu.note: Ogma, Lug, and Dagda receive battle equipment or support from them.

Torcc Triath.note: The king of boars is owned or accompanied by Brigit.

Treblann.note: Donn receives and protects Treblann at Tech Duinn during Fráech’s expedition.

Triall.note: Some learned genealogies assign Triall as Bres’s child, possibly through conflation.

Twrch Trwyth.note: Gwyn is required for Arthur's hunt of the transformed king and monstrous boar.
Manawydan and three companions close upon the enchanted boar and drive him into the Severn.

Túatha Dé.note: The peoples form an alliance through intermarriage and shared descendants.
The Fomorian host battles the Túatha Dé and is routed toward the sea.

Uaithne.note: If Uaithne is a supernatural harper, the Dagda is his master or associate.

Uchtdelbh.note: Áine’s embrace of Manannán prompts Uchtdelbh to notice Aillén and leave Manannán.

Uillenn.note: Uillenn kills Oirbsen, identified with Manannán, before Loch Oirbsen covers his burial place.

Uiscias.note: Uiscias is associated as teacher or guardian with Nuada's irresistible sword.
Uiscias.source: Four Jewels of Túatha Dé Danann

Uiscias.myth: Training in the northern city of Findias
Uiscias.note: Uiscias teaches the Tuatha Dé in Findias.

Viśvakarman.note: Comparative scholarship links the Dagda and Viśvakarman through Sucellus.

Yemo.note: Indo-European scholarship compares Donn with reconstructed Yemo in a first-dead complex.
Yemo.source: Lincoln, The Lord of the Dead

Ynawg.note: Ynawg is among the seven survivors who return with Branwen.

demons.myth: Christian reinterpretation of Cú Chulainn’s visions
demons.note: A Christianizing coda reclassifies apparitions formerly called Sídhe as demonic deception.

fallen or neutral angels.note: Christian folklore sometimes explains the Sídhe as expelled or neutral angels.

provision-stealing magician.note: Lludd confronts the magician responsible for stealing the royal household’s provisions.

the Fir Bolg.note: She helps immobilize and confuse them with mist, fire, and blood.

the Irish gods.note: Anu is collectively called mother of the gods of Ireland.
Anu nourished or fed the Irish gods; no fuller narrative survives.

the Púca.note: Later tellings sometimes group this shape-changing being with the fairy people.

the Wiccan Goddess.note: Modern Wiccan interpretations sometimes absorb the Morrígan into a universal Goddess.

the imperial numina.note: Victoria Brigantia receives dedication alongside the emperors' divine powers.

the sons of Cermait.note: Manannán’s crane bag later passes through the possession of Cermait’s sons.

the three gods of Danu.note: The Dagda, Lug, and Ogma consult or receive equipment from this obscure triad.

the three red riders.note: The living-yet-dead riders travel on Donn’s horses and herald death.

two fighting dragons.note: Lludd intoxicates the battling dragons and buries them at Dinas Emrys.

Áed.note: Áed and Aengus are grouped among the Dagda’s sons.
Áed joins Aengus and Cermait in killing Lug.
Place-lore identifies Áed, later killed by Corchenn, as the Dagda’s son.

Áengus Óg.note: Later traditions variously make Áengus Manannán’s foster-son or ward.
Later narrative networks connect Manannán with Áengus’s equipment and protective magic.

Échtach Esarg.note: A disputed genealogical parsing makes Échtach Esarg his father.

Étan.note: A genealogical tract names the poet Étan as his daughter.

Étaín.note: Aengus shelters and heals Étaín in insect form until Fuamnach disperses her.
She moves between mound society and mortality through transformation and rebirth.

Óengus.note: Bres is indirectly connected because Elcmar visits him during Óengus’s magically concealed conception.
Óengus is the Dagda’s son by Boann.
Óengus obtains the Dagda’s Brú by interpreting “day and night” permanently.
The Dagda advises or assists Óengus in dispossessing Elcmar.
Óengus advises him to conceal gold in the satirist’s food.

Óengus.myth: Winning Brug na Bóinne for a day and night
Óengus.note: He gains permanent possession of Brug na Bóinne through legal wordplay.
